questions.prompt: Explain the difference between let and var in Swift. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: States that let creates a constant whose value cannot change after assignment
States that var creates a variable whose value can change at runtime
Mentions that Apple recommends let by default for safety and clear code intent

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, let declares a constant whose value cannot change after it is assigned. In contrast, var declares a variable whose value can change at runtime. Apple recommends declaring values with let by default. This makes code safer by preventing accidental edits and clarifying developer intent.

questions.prompt: Explain how type inference works in Swift and when you should provide an explicit type annotation instead. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that type inference deduces the type automatically from an initial value
Identifies at least one scenario needing explicit annotations (e.g., delayed initialization, choosing Float over Double, Character over String)
States that Swift remains strictly type-safe even when types are inferred

questions.modelAnswer: Swift uses type inference to determine a value's type automatically by inspecting its initial value at compile time. However, you must provide an explicit type annotation when declaring a constant or variable without an immediate initial value. You also use annotations to request specific types. Examples include choosing Character instead of String, or Float instead of Double.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: The Basics

questions.prompt: Why does Swift refuse to automatically convert an Int to a Double when performing arithmetic? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift is strictly type-safe and avoids implicit type coercion
Explains that requiring explicit conversion prevents subtle bugs and unexpected loss of precision
Mentions that developers must write explicit conversions like Double(count)

questions.modelAnswer: Swift avoids automatic numeric conversion because it is a strictly type-safe language. In languages with implicit coercion, silent conversions can hide calculation errors and cause unexpected loss of precision. Swift forces developers to write explicit conversions like Double(myInt). This ensures that every type change is intentional and visible in code.

questions.prompt: Explain delayed initialization with let in Swift. What rules does the compiler enforce? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that let constants can be declared with a type annotation and assigned later
States that the compiler guarantees the constant is assigned exactly once on all code paths
Mentions that reading the constant before assignment triggers a compile-time error

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, you can declare a let constant with a type annotation without an immediate value. The compiler proves that the constant is assigned exactly once on every possible execution branch before it is read. Attempting to read the constant before this assignment causes a compile error, ensuring safety.

questions.prompt: Why does Apple recommend using let by default across iOS applications? Mention at least two concrete benefits. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Identifies that let prevents unintentional mutations and makes code predictable
Identifies multithreading safety (avoiding data races) or compiler performance optimizations as a second concrete benefit
Mentions that code readability and developer intent improve

questions.modelAnswer: Using let by default makes application state predictable by preventing unintentional mutations throughout your code. It also provides thread safety benefits in concurrent applications by ensuring that shared constant values cannot cause data races. Furthermore, knowing a value never changes allows the Swift compiler to apply deeper performance optimizations.
